implementation_notes: The .NET container is itself the locator: IServiceProvider.GetService(Type) / GetRequiredService<T>() resolves any service registered in the composition root, and the framework makes the provider available to the types it creates (ASP.NET Core request services via HttpContext.RequestServices, hosted services, middleware, minimal-API handlers). Microsoft's own guidance is to avoid resolving from it whenever constructor injection is possible and never to inject a runtime-resolving factory, because that mixes IoC strategies; the accepted use is exactly the place where no injection point exists, where the object's constructor or Initialize method acts as a miniature composition root. Remember the lifetime rules the lookup hides: a scoped service resolved from the root provider is captured for the application lifetime unless scope validation is enabled, and keyed registrations need GetRequiredKeyedService/GetRequiredKeyedService<T>.
pitfalls: Resolving a scoped service from the root provider silently promotes it to application lifetime (the captive dependency); use an injected IServiceScopeFactory or the request's RequestServices and enable scope validation in development.

GetService returns null for an unregistered type while GetRequiredService<T>() throws InvalidOperationException: mixing the two makes misconfiguration visible at some call sites and invisible at others.
Caching an IServiceProvider in a static field recreates the ambient-locator anti-pattern; the provider is a composition-root tool, not a service.

variants.name: Common Service Locator / Prism IServiceLocator
variants.implementation_notes: The classic .NET form, kept alive by Prism and the Common Service Locator library: a framework-agnostic IServiceLocator abstraction with adapters for Unity, MEF and other containers, so a library can resolve what the host provides without binding to one container. Prism uses it for module initialisation and exposes it as an application service; its own guidance says the locator is for library/infrastructure code that must support several containers and is not meant to be the application's general-purpose container. Reach for it only in that multi-container case, and prefer the injected provider variant when one container is fixed.
pitfalls: ServiceLocator.Current throws ActivationException until a container adapter is installed during bootstrap; anything resolved before that point fails at run time.
Two containers in one process resolve through whichever adapter registered last, so scope the locator per host rather than per process.
Using the ambient ServiceLocator from application code mixes it with constructor injection and hides the graph Prism's DI container was configured to make explicit.
